summary.en: Powdery mildew is a group of fungal diseases caused by obligate biotrophic fungi belonging to the order Erysiphales. These pathogens colonize the surfaces of susceptible plant tissues, producing characteristic white to gray fungal growth composed of mycelium and asexual spores. Infection can affect leaves, stems, buds, flowers, and, in some host–pathogen combinations, fruits, resulting in tissue distortion, premature leaf senescence, reduced plant vigor, and diminished crop quality or yield.

favorableConditions.en: Warm, dry days with humid nights

alt.en: White powdery fungal growth covering a green squash leaf

caption.en: Powdery mildew on a squash leaf.

lead.en: Powdery mildew is typically recognized by the development of white to gray, superficial fungal colonies on susceptible plant tissues, particularly leaves and young shoots.

body.en: The fungal colonies consist of surface-growing mycelium and chains of asexual spores (conidia), which give infected tissues their characteristic powdery appearance. Depending on the fungal species and host plant, colonies may develop on either or both leaf surfaces. As infection progresses, affected leaves may exhibit chlorosis, curling, deformation, premature senescence, and abscission. Young shoots, buds, flowers, and fruits may also become infected.

diagnosticNote.en: Powdery mildew fungi are obligate biotrophs that obtain nutrients from living host cells through specialized feeding structures called haustoria. Unlike many other fungal pathogens, their conidia generally do not require free water on plant surfaces for germination and infection.

alt.en: White spotting on a green leaf

caption.en: Early colonies appear as separate white patches.

en: White or gray powder on leaf surfaces

lead.en: Powdery mildew fungi survive between growing seasons through different structures, depending on the pathogen species and host plant. Disease development involves spore production, airborne dispersal, host infection, and repeated cycles of secondary sporulation.

text.en: Mycelium in dormant buds or sexual resting structures (chasmothecia), depending on the species.
Ascospores or conidia reach susceptible plant tissues and initiate infection.
Mycelium develops on the plant surface and forms haustoria within epidermal cells.
Conidia are produced in large numbers and dispersed by air to susceptible tissues.

body.en: Repeated production and dispersal of conidia enable multiple infection cycles during the growing season. Moderate temperatures, high relative humidity, and shaded conditions generally favor disease development, although environmental requirements vary among powdery mildew species.

lead.en: Combine prevention, careful monitoring, and targeted treatment. Begin with cultural controls and intervene early.

intro.en: Start here. Good growing conditions reduce disease pressure and are the foundation of effective management.

en: Space plants for airflow and prune dense interior growth.
Place susceptible plants in adequate sun; avoid excessive shade.
Remove heavily infected leaves and dispose of them away from the garden.
Avoid excess nitrogen, which promotes soft, susceptible growth.

intro.en: Biological products can suppress early infections, but perform best when applied preventively and consistently.

en: Products containing Bacillus subtilis or Bacillus amyloliquefaciens may help protect new growth.
Apply before symptoms become widespread and repeat according to the product label.
Do not combine living microbial products with incompatible fungicides.

intro.en: Fungicides protect healthy tissue; they rarely restore leaves that are already heavily colonized.

en: Horticultural oils, sulfur, and potassium bicarbonate are common low-impact options.
Rotate active ingredients by FRAC group to reduce resistance risk.
Always follow the label, observe temperature restrictions, and confirm the crop is listed.

text.en: The label is the law. Confirm that both the plant and disease are listed, and never apply oil or sulfur to heat-stressed plants.
